title: NvMap::PinHandle never frees anything when SMMU space is exhausted (infinite loop, front() on empty list)
trigger: Guest pins nvmap handles until smmu.Allocate(aligned_up) returns 0 (device address space full or too fragmented). The loop body runs: if unmap_queue is empty, front() on an empty std::list is UB (the LOG_CRITICAL else branch is unreachable); if it is non-empty, UnmapHandle is guarded by handle_description->d_address, which is 0 for a handle that is being newly pinned (d_address is only reset to 0 by UnmapHandle and set after this loop), so nothing is freed and the loop spins forever holding unmap_queue_lock and the handle mutex.
impact: Crash/garbage dereference when the queue is empty, otherwise a permanent hang of the HLE nvdrv thread (and any thread needing unmap_queue_lock). Only when the device address space is exhausted, which is rare.
reasoning: The guard tests the wrong handle: handle_description->d_address is 0 on this path (not in the queue, pins==0, UnmapHandle zeroes it and Map assigns it only after the loop), so UnmapHandle(*freeHandleDesc) is dead and the allocation never succeeds on a retry. front() is called with no empty() check, so the LOG_CRITICAL else is unreachable. The device address space is large, so exhaustion needs heavy pinning or fragmentation; that is why it is narrow, not refuted.
fix_note: Suggested fix is right: check unmap_queue.empty() (return 0/error), test freeHandleDesc->d_address, and UnmapHandle already erases the queue entry. Take care to avoid the lock-order inversion (queue lock then other handle's mutex) which can deadlock against UnpinHandle (handle mutex then queue lock); use try_lock or release the pinned handle's mutex.

title: IocCtrlEventWait writes events[event_id] out of bounds on the early BadParameter return
trigger: Guest issues the non-allocation nvhost-ctrl EventWait ioctl (is_allocation=false) with params.value.raw >= 64 (e.g. 0x10000000) and any fence that returns early before must_unmark_fail is cleared: fence.id >= MaxSyncPoints (BadParameter), fence.value == 0, fence already signalled, or UpdateMin signalled. SCOPE_EXIT then executes events[event_id].fails = 0 with event_id up to 2^32-1.
impact: Out-of-bounds 4-byte zero write at events + event_id*sizeof(InternalEvent) in host memory: access violation (crash) or heap/object corruption; written without events_mutex. Needs a malformed guest request.
reasoning: event_id is copied from guest data before any validation, the scope exit is armed with must_unmark_fail = !is_allocation, and the slot >= MaxNvEvents check only occurs after must_unmark_fail = false. Every early return before that point (not only BadParameter; also the three Success returns) runs the unchecked write. Correctly formed guests pass a valid slot so they are unaffected.
fix_note: Suggested fix is right: reject event_id >= MaxNvEvents up front (when !is_allocation) or arm the cleanup only after the slot is validated. Also take NvEventsLock for the write; note the lock is taken later at line 139, so the scope-exit write on early paths is unlocked even for valid slots (benign race on a u32).

title: SharedBufferSession::presentation_slot_base is never assigned, so two sessions use the same pool slots
trigger: Two different processes (distinct aruids) call CreateSharedLayerSession on the ManagerDisplayService while both sessions are alive. Both sessions get presentation_slot_base 0 so their producers map to pool slots 3 and 4 of the same shared buffer.
impact: Both layers present from/into the same shared-buffer memory: frames overwrite each other (wrong image in the shared layer). Does nothing with a single session; only 2 sessions are supported by the pool, and a third has no slots at all. Normally one session exists.
reasoning: Grep of the vi directory shows presentation_slot_base only read (GetPresentationSlot in CreateSession, dequeue and GetProducerSlot), never written, and CreateSession only rejects a duplicate aruid, with no cap of SharedBufferMaxSessions. The pool is sized for two sessions, so the design intent was a per-session base. In practice a single process (the running title) uses it.
fix_note: Suggested fix is right (base = free-slot-index * SharedBufferSlotsPerSession, freed in DestroySession) and should also reject when 2 sessions already exist (return an error) since the pool has no room for a third.

title: IocCtrlEventWait blocks the HLE thread in an unbounded host wait while holding events_mutex
trigger: Guest cancels (IocCtrlEventSignal increments event.fails) the same nvhost event 3 times, then calls EventWait on that slot (or timeout==0 poll) with a fence value the GPU never reaches, e.g. a fence whose increment is queued behind work that another guest thread has not submitted yet. check_failing then calls StallApplication (suspending guest threads) and WaitHost with no timeout, with events_mutex held.
impact: Permanent hang of the nvhost-ctrl service thread, the suspended guest, and every other nvhost-ctrl event ioctl (all wait on events_mutex). Only for fences that never get reached; normal NVN fences are for already-submitted work so the wait ends.
reasoning: Structurally as described: WaitHost -> Wait does wait_cv.wait(lk, pred) with no timeout, called inside check_failing while `lock = NvEventsLock()` (line 139) is held and the application is stalled (emulation suspended, so no guest thread can make progress that would produce the missing increment). The fails counter is guest-driven (EventSignal), so a trigger exists, but it requires a fence that the GPU genuinely cannot reach, which is a guest/emulation fault case. It appears to be a deliberate wait-for-GPU strategy rather than an accident.
fix_note: A bounded wait (e.g. wait_for with a few hundred ms then fall through to the normal Timeout return) and releasing events_mutex before waiting would be safe; unbounded waiting is intentional for latency, so choose a generous bound to avoid reintroducing spurious timeouts.
